claims.text: Chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys delays dislocation nucleation under uniaxial tension.
Chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys delays dislocation motion under uniaxial tension.
The delay in dislocation nucleation and motion depends on crystallographic loading orientation.
The delay in dislocation nucleation and motion depends on thermal activation.
Delayed dislocation activity increases the initial elastic regime relative to chemically simpler alloys.
Delayed dislocation activity enhances strain hardening at high strain rates relative to chemically simpler alloys.
Local lattice distortions in a high-entropy alloy act as barriers or modulators of dislocation nucleation and propagation.
Local chemical inhomogeneities in a high-entropy alloy act as barriers or modulators of dislocation nucleation and propagation.
The disordered atomic arrangement increases the activation energy for dislocation nucleation in specific crystallographic directions.
The disorder-induced increase in dislocation-nucleation activation energy is more pronounced at high strain rates because thermal activation is limited.
Temperature modulates the disorder-induced delay in dislocation nucleation.
Delayed plasticity onset temporarily raises yield strength.
At high strain rates, the high-entropy alloy will have a higher apparent elastic limit than a chemically simpler alloy with similar crystal symmetry.
At high strain rates, the high-entropy alloy will begin plastic deformation later than the chemically simpler baseline.
The high-entropy alloy will display a later and more pronounced yield point than the chemically simpler baseline.
The predicted differences in elastic limit and plasticity onset will vary with loading direction and temperature.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply while the high-entropy alloy remains single phase.
A simulation cell must be sufficiently large to capture the relevant dislocation mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to uniaxial tensile deformation over temperatures where thermal activation remains relevant and strain rates where inertial effects are significant.
The quantitative delay in nucleation and its effect on yield strength may depend on simulation scale and interatomic-potential accuracy, and extrapolation to experimental scales is uncertain.
